articles.full_text:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC)
Largest market share, serves Apple, Nvidia, AMD
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Semiconductor Foundry market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global semiconductor foundry market is entering a phase of structural transformation, driven by the proliferation of AI workloads, the electrification of automotive platforms, and the imperative for supply chain resilience. Foundries are no longer mere manufacturers; they are strategic partners in design ecosystems, offering process design kits, IP libraries, and advanced packaging that enable chiplet-based architectures. Demand is bifurcating: leading-edge nodes (below 7nm) serve high-performance computing and AI accelerators, while mature nodes (28nm and above) cater to automotive, industrial, and IoT applications with long lifecycles.
This divergence creates distinct competitive dynamics, capital intensity, and qualification hurdles. Geopolitical factors are prompting regional capacity investments, particularly in the US, Europe, and Japan, aiming to reduce concentration in East Asia. The market is forecast to grow at a robust CAGR through 2035, with advanced packaging and heterogeneous integration becoming key value drivers. However, restraints such as high capital expenditure, talent shortages, and export controls on advanced equipment could temper growth.
This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering demand drivers, end-use sectors, regional outlooks, and competitive strategies.
The baseline scenario for the semiconductor foundry market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates sustained expansion, albeit with cyclical fluctuations. The primary growth engine is the insatiable demand for compute power, fueled by AI training and inference, cloud services, and edge intelligence. This drives leading-edge foundry capacity, where technological leadership confers pricing power. Simultaneously, the automotive sector's transition to electric and autonomous vehicles multiplies semiconductor content per vehicle, boosting demand for mature and specialty nodes. Industrial automation, 5G/6G infrastructure, and consumer electronics further underpin volume.
The market is expected to grow at a CAGR of 7.2% during the forecast period, reaching a market index of 185 by 2035 (2025=100). This growth is not uniform: advanced nodes will outpace mature nodes in revenue terms, but mature nodes will see stable unit demand. Supply chain regionalization will lead to duplicate capacity, potentially exerting downward pressure on utilization rates in some regions. Pricing will remain firm at the leading edge due to scarcity, while mature nodes face competitive pressure. The industry's capital intensity will remain high, with annual capex exceeding $100 billion collectively, directed at new fabs, EUV lithography, and advanced packaging facilities.
The risk of overcapacity in mature nodes is balanced by long-term demand growth and government incentives. Overall, the outlook is positive, with foundries that can offer differentiated technology, design support, and supply assurance best positioned to capture value.
Consumer electronics remains the largest end-use sector for semiconductor foundries, encompassing smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables, and smart home devices. Currently, demand is driven by the replacement cycle of 5G smartphones and the proliferation of AI-enabled features, which require more advanced processors and power management ICs. Through 2035, the sector will see a shift towards more integrated and power-efficient designs, with foundries providing advanced nodes for application processors and mature nodes for peripheral chips. The demand-side indicators to watch include global smartphone shipments, PC replacement rates, and the adoption of AR/VR devices.
As device makers increasingly differentiate through custom silicon, foundries that offer design support and IP portfolios will benefit. However, growth will be tempered by market saturation in developed regions and lengthening replacement cycles. The sector's share of foundry revenue will gradually decline as automotive and industrial applications grow faster, but it will remain a cornerstone of volume demand. Current trend: Moderate growth, driven by smartphones, PCs, and wearables, with increasing silicon content per device..
Major trends: Integration of AI accelerators into smartphones and PCs, driving demand for advanced nodes, Proliferation of custom silicon for wearables and smart home devices, Shift to 3nm and 2nm process technologies for flagship mobile processors, Increasing use of chiplets and advanced packaging in high-end consumer devices, and Growth in demand for power management ICs and sensors for battery-powered devices.
Representative participants: Apple, Samsung Electronics, Xiaomi, Lenovo, Huawei, and Sony.
The automotive sector is undergoing a seismic shift towards electric vehicles (EVs) and autonomous driving, dramatically increasing semiconductor content per vehicle. Currently, a typical EV contains twice as many semiconductors as an internal combustion engine vehicle, with demand spanning power semiconductors (SiC, GaN), microcontrollers, sensors, and infotainment processors. Through 2035, the adoption of ADAS and eventually fully autonomous vehicles will require high-performance computing platforms, LiDAR, and radar chips, driving demand for advanced nodes. However, automotive-grade chips demand stringent reliability and qualification, often taking 18-36 months, creating high barriers for foundries.
Demand-side indicators include EV sales penetration, ADAS feature adoption rates, and government regulations on emissions and safety. Foundries with automotive-specific process design kits and long-term supply agreements will capture value. The sector's share of foundry revenue will rise significantly, making it a key growth engine. Current trend: Rapid growth, fueled by electrification, autonomous driving, and in-vehicle connectivity..
Major trends: Electrification driving demand for SiC and GaN power devices, ADAS and autonomous driving requiring high-performance compute and sensor fusion, Software-defined vehicles increasing demand for centralized computing architectures, Stringent safety and reliability standards (ISO 26262) shaping foundry qualifications, and Regionalization of automotive supply chains to ensure resilience.
Representative participants: Tesla, Volkswagen, Toyota, General Motors, Bosch, and Continental.
The industrial sector encompasses a broad range of applications, including factory automation, robotics, power management, and industrial IoT. Currently, demand is driven by the need for efficient motor control, real-time sensing, and connectivity in smart factories. Through 2035, the industrial internet of things (IIoT) will connect millions of devices, requiring low-power, reliable semiconductors. Foundries serving this sector focus on mature nodes (28nm and above) and specialty processes like BCD and high-voltage. Demand-side indicators include industrial robot installations, manufacturing PMI, and investment in smart infrastructure.
The sector values longevity, reliability, and supply assurance over cutting-edge performance, leading to long-term partnerships with foundries. As industrial automation accelerates, the demand for microcontrollers, analog ICs, and power discretes will grow, providing stable revenue for foundries with mature-node capacity. Current trend: Steady growth, driven by automation, robotics, and industrial IoT..
Major trends: Growth in industrial robotics and collaborative robots, Adoption of IIoT for predictive maintenance and process optimization, Increasing demand for energy-efficient power semiconductors, Shift towards edge computing in industrial environments, and Need for ruggedized and high-reliability components.
Representative participants: Siemens, ABB, Rockwell Automation, Schneider Electric, Honeywell, and Mitsubishi Electric.
The communication sector includes smartphones, networking equipment, data center switches, and telecom infrastructure. Currently, the rollout of 5G networks is driving demand for RF front-end modules, baseband processors, and high-speed networking chips. Through 2035, the advent of 6G and the exponential growth of data traffic will necessitate advanced nodes for high-performance networking and optical communication. Data center expansion, driven by cloud and AI, will require high-bandwidth memory and switching chips. Demand-side indicators include global data traffic, 5G subscription rates, and data center capex. Foundries with advanced RF and high-speed process technologies will benefit.
The sector is characterized by rapid technology cycles and high design-in costs, favoring foundries with strong IP and design support. As communication networks become more virtualized and software-defined, the demand for custom silicon will rise. articles.title: TSMC and Samsung reveal High-NA EUV plans as Intel moves into early production - Sammy Fans
articles.summary: TSMC and Samsung reveal High-NA EUV plans as Intel moves into early production  Sammy Fans
articles.full_text:
TSMC, Samsung, Intel, and SK Hynix are preparing to use a new technology, High-NA EUV, to make advanced computer chips. High-NA EUV is a powerful machine that can print very small designs on chips.
TSMC plans to use High-NA EUV for large-scale production of logic chips from 2030. Until then, it plans to continue using current EUV technology on its 2029 roadmap. This shows that TSMC is taking a careful approach to the new technology.
Samsung aims to use High-NA EUV earlier, starting with DRAM memory production in 2028. DRAM is a type of memory used in computers, smartphones and other electronic devices. SK Hynix is also expected to use the technology for DRAM around 2028, according to later reports.
Intel has already started using High-NA EUV. In July 2026, the company said it had begun production with the new machine. Intel is using it on some layers of its Panther Lake chips. However, the technology is still being used only on selected layers.
High-NA EUV machines are made by ASML. They have bigger mirrors than older EUV machines. This helps chipmakers print smaller designs and may reduce the number of steps needed to make some parts of a chip.
The companies are also looking at changing from 6-inch to 12-inch photomasks. Photomasks carry the chip design used during manufacturing. Bigger masks could help produce more chips in less time. However, announced dates are plans, and they do not always mean full production will begin exactly on those dates.
Samsung is warning that the rapid expansion of High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) for AI infrastructure could put additional pressure on conventional DRAM supply in 2027.
According to Reuters, Samsung Executive Vice President Kim Taewoo said that HBM could consume nearly 30% of the DRAM industry’s wafer capacity in the year 2027, compared with around 20% currently.
HBM and conventional DRAM rely on the same underlying wafer production resources, meaning a larger HBM allocation can leave less capacity for standard memory.
Samsung has already increased its focus on this market. The company began mass-producing HBM4 in February 2026 and has since moved to HBM4E sampling, while also preparing custom HBM products for 2027.
Samsung Electronics Executive Vice President Kim Taewoo said HBM and standard DRAM compete for the same wafer capacity, meaning expanding HBM output could constrain standard DRAM supply.
The comments highlight a potential trade-off for the memory industry. As vendors redirect more wafer capacity toward higher-value HBM products, supplies of conventional DRAM used in PCs, phones and servers could become tighter.
Samsung itself expects HBM sales to more than triple in 2026 compared with 2025, underscoring how quickly AI memory is becoming a larger part of its business.
Samsung Foundry appears to be making measurable progress with its 2nm chip manufacturing technology, with a fresh industry report indicating that the yield of its first-generation SF2 process is now approaching 60%.
According to Chosun, Samsung Foundry has lifted SF2 yield to around the 60% level, up from the mid-50% range previously reported by the market.
Higher yields generally make an advanced process more commercially viable and give foundries greater confidence when taking on high-volume customer orders.
Samsung introduced SF2 as its first-generation 2nm process using a Gate-All-Around transistor architecture. The technology is already being used for the Exynos 2600, which powers select Galaxy S26 models.
While improving yield is important, Samsung now needs to demonstrate that SF2 can deliver competitive power efficiency and performance consistently in customer products.
The company is reportedly working with potential customers to evaluate areas such as heat generation and power consumption before expanding its 2nm business.
Samsung’s second-generation SF2P process is particularly important. Industry reports have indicated that SF2P can deliver up to 12% higher performance, 25% lower power consumption, and an 8% smaller area compared with SF2.
The reported yield improvement does not immediately change the competitive landscape. Samsung still needs to convert process improvements into sustained production quality, customer confidence, and large orders.
However, approaching the 60% yield mark gives Samsung a stronger foundation as it pushes SF2P and future 2nm variants toward broader adoption.
In case Samsung can combine improving yields with better power efficiency, its advanced-node foundry business could become increasingly relevant to major chip designers over the next few years.
Samsung is reportedly moving faster than previously planned with the expansion of its Pyeongtaek Campus 5 (P5), bringing high-value DRAM and HBM production equipment into the facility earlier than expected.
According to Semiconductor Insider, Samsung is reportedly looking to begin moving equipment into the first production phase of P5 (Ph1) around May or June 2027, instead of the previously expected July or August timeframe.
P5 is being developed as one of Samsung’s next-generation semiconductor manufacturing hubs, with the broader facility expected to become operational from 2028.
Samsung appears to be preparing Ph1 primarily for DRAM and HBM production, positioning the facility to handle the growing demand coming from AI servers and accelerators.
In its second-quarter 2026 results, Samsung said server DRAM, HBM and enterprise SSD demand should remain strong as AI infrastructure investment expands. The company also reported record quarterly performance from its Memory Business.
The reported P5 roadmap extends beyond its first phase. Samsung is also discussing preparations for Ph2, which could eventually focus on advanced NAND production, although formal purchase orders have reportedly not been issued yet.
For Samsung, accelerating P5 is therefore about more than simply adding factory space. The company is preparing capacity around the products (DRAM, HBM, and enterprise SSD) expected to remain central to AI infrastructure.
Qualcomm praised Samsung Electronics, saying it is the “strongest partner worldwide” in the mobile business, and confirmed that its Foundry’s 2nm chip technology is under consideration for future Snapdragon products.
Chris Patrick, Qualcomm’s SVP and general manager of mobile handsets, said during discussions with Korean media that the company is closely evaluating Samsung Foundry’s 2nm technology for potential use in future products.
Importantly, Qualcomm has not reached the point of naming a Snapdragon chip that will use Samsung’s process. The company is still working to understand how the technology could be applied to its future designs.
That leaves the door open for Samsung to become a future manufacturing partner for Snapdragon flagship platforms, alongside TSMC.
Qualcomm has just introduced the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, its newest premium mobile platforms built around a 2nm process.
For Samsung Foundry, Qualcomm’s evaluation could become an important opportunity. Samsung says its SF2 process entered mass production in 2025, while its second-generation 2nm technology is being developed for newer mobile, HPC and AI applications.
Samsung has also said that its foundry business is seeing growing 2nm engagements, including projects involving major US customers.
Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips are used across a large number of premium Android phones, giving Samsung Foundry a route to compete more directly for some of the industry’s highest-profile mobile silicon designs.
At Snapdragon Summit 2026, Qualcomm also highlighted its latest Snapdragon platforms as the foundation for more capable on-device and agentic AI experiences.
Samsung is looking beyond conventional 2D chip layouts as it explores a way to 3D vertically stack memory elements inside superconducting quantum processors.
The approach is detailed in a Samsung patent titled “Superconducting qubit memory of quantum computer,” granted in South Korea in 2025, with corresponding US patents.
Samsung’s 3D approach to quantum memory
Samsung’s patented design focuses on superconducting qubits, where the computing element, known as a transmon, works alongside a superconducting resonator that stores quantum information.
The patent (via ETNews) proposes a layered structure for the resonator rather than keeping all components on a single plane.
It describes superconducting waveguide layers separated by insulating material, with additional superconducting layers forming the stack. The patented waveguide layer can include a superconducting resonator.
A potential path toward larger quantum processors
Samsung’s interest is particularly notable because the company is already researching scalable superconducting quantum processors.
SAIT says it is developing an integrated quantum processing unit combining a superconducting multi-qubit chip with a cryogenic CMOS control chip, with the goal of building scalable, reliable fault-tolerant systems.
The newly highlighted patent should therefore be viewed as part of a longer research effort rather than evidence that Samsung is preparing a commercial quantum computer.
The patent’s priority date goes back to November 2020, while the Korean patent was granted in March 2025. US members of the patent family were also granted in 2024 and 2025.
If quantum processors eventually require dramatically larger numbers of qubits, chip area, signal routing and interference will become increasingly important engineering challenges. A 3D memory architecture could give Samsung another option for addressing those constraints.
For now, this is best understood as Samsung securing intellectual property around a potential building block for future quantum computing, while continuing its broader research into scalable quantum hardware.

articles.title: Trump says tech CEOs signed ‘morally binding’ document to self-regulate artificial intelligence - Washington Examiner
articles.summary: Trump says tech CEOs signed ‘morally binding’ document to self-regulate artificial intelligence  Washington Examiner
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump told reporters in a rare impromptu press conference outside of the White House that he and technology CEOs signed a “morally binding” agreement to self-regulate artificial intelligence as public fears mount about the technology’s development.
Although Trump conceded that the “White House Accord on Superintelligence: A Joint Commitment on Frontier SI Responsibilities” is not binding, he compared it to a constitution.
“It’s almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest and the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection,” he said.
Trump also mentioned a committee to manage AI development, but it is unclear whether that is different from the task force and czar he announced last week, though the president added he would name the czar in “the next three or four days.”
Trump appeared alongside House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) and tech CEOs outside the West Wing, from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, who have publicly supported regulations, in addition to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who have opposed them.
For Johnson, the agreement was a statement of principles, standards, expectations, and “commitments that are voluntary on behalf of the industry.”
“It’s, in short summary, robust internal controls and layers of internal and external review,” he said. “That’s important because you need people to be providing oversight and transparency, and that’s what these leaders are going to do. The White House and Congress will continue to guide the industry’s development in a safe manner because we owe that to the American people, and we will do it.”
Amodei, who has led the calls for a coordinated slowdown in AI frontier model development, told reporters that he continued to consider the technology to have “very real risks.”
“The mechanism [of] how we address those risks is still under discussion, but we all need to work, we all need to work together to make sure that we can win and we can win safely,” he said. “If we do this right, we work with the president and everyone here, we can win safely.”
At the same time, Trump, during the same press conference, remained adamant that Democrats’ concerns about AI safety were a “hoax.”
“I think they would love to see it shut down, just like it was a hoax for 12 years for global warming,” he said. “What I am calling a hoax is what the Democrats do, because they don’t want to see it be successful, because they think that’s bad for Republicans.”

In September 2026, China's commercial aerospace sector entered a period of intensive explosive growth, with multiple companies completing financing totaling hundreds of millions of yuan, and at least 10 space launches conducted within a single month, sending 44 satellites into orbit.
The combined heat of capital and intensive launches points to one trend: commercial aerospace is shifting from the technology verification phase to large-scale deployment. However, the more satellites are launched, the closer the industry gets to the limit of the "space-sensing and ground-computing" path, which further drives the industry's attention to and layout of space computing.
On September 25, the launch ceremony of the "String of Space" computing constellation program was held in Hangzhou. According to the thousand-satellite roadmap announced on site, this space computing constellation, the first in China targeting the global market, is planned to deploy more than 1,000 space agents in the long term, and the G1 satellite is scheduled to be launched in 2027, with a computing load of 11.5KW and computing power of 40-60P (calculated based on existing computing power standards).

The "String of Space" computing constellation is jointly promoted and constructed by Earthii, co-builder of the Trisomy Computing Constellation, and Oriental Starlink. Oriental Starlink is responsible for the overall design and operation, while Earthii provides AI capability support and expands the international market, promoting the connection of "AI + aerospace" technology with global digital service demands.
Founded in 2021, Earthii is committed to building a space computing network, providing services including space computing systems, intelligent satellites, on-orbit constellation operation, and AI + big data applications.
Song Bingchen, co-founder of Oriental Starlink, told 36Kr that the goal Earthii has set for itself is to create an integrated space agent that integrates chips, algorithms and models, "becoming a space computing node that can think, make decisions and evolve."
At present, Earthii's business has expanded to more than 40 countries around the world, making it the first private commercial aerospace enterprise in China to realize overseas delivery of satellites and ground systems. The company's revenue reached 130 million yuan in 2025, with overseas market revenue accounting for more than half and realizing profitability.
1. Build an integrated space agent that integrates chips, algorithms and models
On August 5 this year, the first reasoning verification satellite of the "String of Space" computing constellation - "Oriental Starlink 05/06" (Oriental Huiyan Hyperspectral AI Twin Satellites), carrying the self-developed "String" AI on-board computing platform of Earthii, was successfully launched by the JL-3 Y12 carrier rocket.
In August 2023, the "Earthii Intelligent Emergency No.1" carrying the first-generation "String" platform was launched into orbit, with a computing power of 60TOPS at that time. It realized on-satellite real-time observation, real-time processing and space intelligence through more than 100 algorithms, eliminated invalid data, and then transmitted the calculation results back to the ground. Taking satellite images of 10,000 square kilometers as an example, the traditional satellite method takes 180 days, while the intelligent satellite only needs several hours of on-orbit processing to complete dynamic target extraction.
In 2024, the computing power of the "String" platform was further increased to 400TOPS. However, to raise the single-satellite computing power to more than 400TOPS, it is necessary to systematically solve the problems of increased energy consumption and heat dissipation caused by synchronization in engineering.
In the vacuum environment of space, chips can only dissipate heat through radiation. Therefore, Earthii independently developed high thermal conductivity composite materials, which increases the thermal conductivity to several times that of aluminum alloys, and is used in conjunction with deployable radiators. Song Bingchen revealed that in the future, Earthii will also introduce self-developed heat pump technology to further improve the heat dissipation capacity of space servers.
The founder of Earthii once said frankly, "At present, whether in terms of rocket technology, mass satellite production capacity or capital scale, we are not at the same level as SpaceX."
To realize the thousand-satellite blueprint, Earthii plans to make continuous breakthroughs in three technical routes: first, cooperate with domestic manufacturers to develop radiation-resistant chips, and it is expected to deploy the world's first reconfigurable chip with Qingwei Intelligence by the end of this year; second, explore new materials such as perovskite to improve the conversion efficiency of solar panels; third, deploy the first domestic space liquid-cooled agent next year to optimize the heat dissipation performance of satellites.
2. Remote sensing first then computing, from regional commercial use to global commercial use
As of June 2026, the 6 satellites of the two companies have a maximum cumulative in-orbit time of more than 2600 days, accumulating a large amount of actual performance data of chips in the space radiation environment.
In the past few years, the domestic space computing power market has not yet achieved a commercial closed loop as a whole. Therefore, Earthii chose to make money with mature remote sensing data services to accumulate customers and trust, and then gradually cultivate and superimpose space computing capabilities. Due to the limited demand in the domestic remote sensing satellite market, and the team has a group of talents from ZTE with more than ten years of overseas market experience, the overseas market has become the primary priority for Earthii to realize marketization.
"Many countries in the Middle East, Central Asia and Southeast Asia are also eager to build their own aerospace capabilities and space sovereignty." Song Bingchen said, By adopting the combination of "whole satellite export + data service + talent training", Earthii cuts into the niche market of the third world countries, which is ignored by the traditional European and American aerospace system, but has strong willingness to pay and relatively less fierce competition.
On November 11, 2024, Earthii delivered the first "OmanSat" to Oman. This intelligent remote sensing satellite is mainly loaded with an optical camera with a panchromatic resolution of 1 meter and a multispectral resolution of 4 meters, and has the capability of continuous push-broom imaging for up to 45 minutes. It can be applied to fields such as land detailed survey, urban planning, forest survey, and disaster monitoring.

After two months of in-orbit operation, "OmanSat" has flown more than 1200 circles around the earth, completed more than 300 measurement and control tasks and more than 100 data transmission tasks, received about 3000GB of data, and successfully realized the first space practice verification of on-orbit AI identification of ships and aircraft, space-based distributed operating system and space-based remote sensing large model, as well as the satellite-ground network interconnection.
"No private company in China has ever done satellite export. We are not crossing the river by feeling the stones, we can't even feel the stones." From contacting customers, demand docking, scheme design, satellite development, launch coordination, in-orbit testing, to the final successful launch of "OmanSat", Earthii spent nearly two years, running through the whole process from satellite export approval, in-orbit delivery to foreign exchange settlement. "It is equivalent to opening up a commercial path that did not exist before."
The success of "OmanSat" was included in the middle school textbooks of Oman, and it also became a stepping stone for Earthii to open up more overseas markets. Since then, its business has expanded to Indonesia, Uzbekistan, Turkey, and more than 40 countries in southern Africa and Central Asia.
In the process of serving more sovereign countries, Earthii provides product combinations adapted to local needs according to the differentiated demands of different continents and regions. For example, countries in the Middle East have relatively sufficient funds, pay more attention to sovereign capabilities, and need whole-satellite export and talent training; Southeast Asian countries focus on livelihood applications such as agriculture and fisheries, and mainly purchase data and services; Africa attaches great importance to disaster early warning and resource management.
Song Bingchen concluded that the core competitiveness behind the differentiated service of "satellite going global" lies in three points: Technical strength is the admission ticket, delivery capability is the foundation of trust, and long-term operation builds trust relationships.
Compliance is the prerequisite and lifeline of all the above. "The particularity of this industry determines that we would rather lose customers than cross the red line." Song Bingchen said that Earthii will carry out a complete set of internal training from post training, delivery internal control to audit specifications, all services go through formal national approval, and do not involve sensitive fields such as military affairs.

articles.title: TechInsights Teardown Confirms TSMC 2nm Nanosheet Transistors Now Inside iPhone 18 Pro - Tech Times
articles.summary: TechInsights Teardown Confirms TSMC 2nm Nanosheet Transistors Now Inside iPhone 18 Pro  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Analyst firm TechInsights published the first independent technical analysis of Apple's A20 Pro processor on September 22, 2026 — and for the semiconductor industry, the significance goes well beyond a single iPhone chip. Until that report, every performance figure attached to TSMC's 2-nanometer N2 process node — the 15 percent speed gain, the 30 percent power reduction, the 1.15× logic density increase over the prior 3nm generation — existed solely as the foundry's own characterization data presented at academic conferences. TechInsights has now extracted the A20 Pro from an iPhone 18 Pro, independently measured production silicon, and published preliminary findings that transform those claims from foundry-asserted to independently validated. Every competitor building a 2nm-class chip now has an external benchmark to meet.
From Fin to Nanosheet: What Gate-All-Around Actually Changes
The headline finding is architectural. TechInsights confirmed that the A20 Pro deploys gate-all-around nanosheet transistors — a fundamental structural departure from the FinFET technology that has defined leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing since Intel introduced it in the early 2010s. ASML's public documentation on GAA vs. FinFET design explains the underlying principle: whereas a FinFET gate wraps around a vertical silicon fin on three sides, leaving one face of the conducting channel exposed, gate-all-around nanosheets enclose the channel on all four sides simultaneously.
In a FinFET, that exposed face becomes an increasingly costly limitation as geometries shrink and off-state leakage current grows harder to control. TSMC's N2 nanosheet architecture replaces those vertical fins with horizontal stacked silicon ribbons, allowing the gate to enclose the channel on all four sides simultaneously. The result is stronger electrostatic control and reduced leakage. The IEEE Spectrum TSMC IEDM 2024 report documents these architectural changes in detail.
The design also introduces manufacturing flexibility unavailable in the FinFET era. In a FinFET, drive current is adjusted only in coarse increments by multiplying the number of fins — one, two, or three. TSMC's implementation, branded NanoFlex, allows nanosheet width to vary across logic cells on the same die, effectively enabling fractional-fin gradations, as the IEEE Spectrum N2 coverage describes. High-performance CPU cores can use wider nanosheets for maximum drive current; efficiency cores and general logic use narrower ones. The same wafer contains both, tuned at the cell level.
One structural detail in TechInsights' early findings carries particular weight for process engineers: TSMC integrates inner spacers in nanosheet channels — a dielectric material placed between the nanosheet channels and the source/drain regions. Inner spacers suppress leakage and improve long-term scaling headroom by enhancing isolation between the gate and source/drain parasitic capacitance. TechInsights flags this as a structural differentiator between TSMC's N2 implementation and competing GAA approaches.
Fabricating these structures requires substantially more complex process steps than FinFETs. Nanosheet formation begins with depositing alternating layers of silicon and silicon-germanium, then selectively etching away the silicon-germanium to leave suspended silicon ribbon channels that gate material subsequently surrounds. The difficulty of that selective removal — at dimensions measured in single-digit nanometers — is one reason TSMC's Geoffrey Yeap, vice president of R&D and advanced technology, described N2 as four years of work at the 2024 IEEE International Electron Devices Meeting.
What Does 2nm Actually Mean?
A brief orientation is warranted. The "2-nanometer" label is a process-generation designation, not a measurement of any single physical feature on the chip. Modern node names stopped corresponding to literal transistor dimensions more than a decade ago; the number signals relative capability improvements in density, performance, and power efficiency compared to the prior generation. What those improvements actually look like in production silicon is determined by independent measurement — which is what makes TechInsights' analysis consequential.
TSMC's own data from the IEDM 2024 conference document N2 performance gains over N3E: up to 15 percent faster at identical power, or up to 30 percent more efficient at identical speed, combined with a logic density increase of more than 1.15×. An enhanced variant, N2P, is scheduled to enter mass production in the second half of 2026, with TSMC's official N2P roadmap projecting roughly 18 percent additional speed or 36 percent additional efficiency improvement relative to N3E.
TechInsights' exploratory analysis specifically notes that the A20 Pro uses aggressively scaled nanosheet logic cells. The complete subscriber report will provide transistor-level measurements — critical dimensions, gate pitch, SRAM cell density — that will constitute the definitive external record of what TSMC N2 produces in production silicon.
Inside the Die: Same Footprint, More Compute
TechInsights' preliminary floorplan analysis places the A20 Pro compute die at approximately 8.0 mm by 12.3 mm (0.31 by 0.48 inches), yielding an estimated A20 Pro die area of 98.2 mm² (0.152 square inches) — nearly identical to the A19 Pro it replaces. That Apple maintained essentially the same die footprint despite a generational process shrink is itself a choice: N2's density gains are being spent on additional compute rather than a smaller die.
TechInsights confirmed a six-core CPU — two high-performance cores with dedicated L2 cache each, and four efficiency cores sharing cache across multiple banks. The A20 Pro GPU core count expands to seven cores, one more than the previous generation.
The most structurally significant expansion is in neural processing. Apple claims doubled AI chip performance over the A19 Pro, and TechInsights' preliminary floorplan analysis confirms that the neural processing area has grown substantially relative to the prior generation. The chip carries dual 16-core Neural Engines alongside Neural Accelerators integrated directly within the CPU complex — a distributed architecture that routes AI workloads to compute throughout the die rather than funneling them through a single centralized block. Apple also claims 50 percent more memory bandwidth in the A20 Pro relative to the A19 Pro — a figure that points toward the packaging shift documented in the next section.
Why Apple Moved the Memory Sideways
For years, Apple stacked LPDDR memory directly atop the application processor die in a package-on-package arrangement, placing memory above the chip in a compact vertical footprint. The A20 Pro abandons that vertical stack.
TechInsights' preliminary analysis identifies a WMCM side-by-side package in which the processor and DRAM are positioned side by side within the same wafer-level package rather than vertically stacked. Preliminary analysis points to a 96-bit LPDDR5X memory interface — a wider memory bus than a vertical stack arrangement could practically accommodate without significant signal-routing complexity.
The motivation for this shift is threefold. Positioning memory beside the processor rather than above it removes the memory's thermal load from the chip's hottest region — a persistent constraint in mobile package-on-package designs. A side-by-side layout physically enables a wider memory interface without stacking-imposed signal-routing penalties. And at the wafer level, integrating two die side by side allows each component to be tested independently before assembly, which can improve overall package yield.
Apple's redesigned vapor chamber cooling system — which the company says provides 3x more surface area than the iPhone 17 Pro's and up to 40 percent better sustained performance — is partly enabled by this packaging shift, which eliminates the memory as an obstacle between the chip and its cooling surface.
Supply chain reports from late 2025 confirmed Apple secured TSMC 2nm majority capacity for 2026, covering the A20 and A20 Pro for the iPhone 18 line as well as M6 chips for the next MacBook Pro generation and R2 chips for a refreshed Vision Pro. TSMC's production facilities in Baoshan and Kaohsiung, Taiwan, were producing approximately 50,000 N2 wafers per month at the production launch, with capacity projected to reach 100,000 wafers per month by the end of 2026. Those wafers carry a $30,000 N2 wafer price — roughly double the price of TSMC's 3nm wafers — reflecting both the process complexity and the captive demand from Apple and other early customers.
Is TSMC N2 the Strongest 2nm Process Now in Production?
TSMC is not the only foundry to have introduced a 2nm-class gate-all-around process. The comparison with Samsung and Intel illuminates both where TSMC leads at scale and where rivals are making different architectural bets.
Samsung was technically first to deploy gate-all-around transistors commercially, beginning with its SF3 3nm process in 2022. Its SF2 2nm process entered mass production in late 2025, producing the Exynos 2600 chip for the Samsung Galaxy S26. Independent reports indicate Samsung SF2 yields crossed 50 percent in January 2026. TSMC's N2 yields, by contrast, were placed well above 60 to 70 percent by Ming-Chi Kuo's yield analysis of TF International Securities as early as spring 2025 and continued to improve through the production ramp. On the process architecture side, TechInsights' early findings flag TSMC's inner spacers versus Samsung — a distinction with implications for leakage control and scalability that the full October report will quantify.

articles.title: Building The Muscle For Tech Sovereignty: Critical Minerals Must Underpin India’s Semiconductor and Manufacturing Ambition - Swarajya
articles.summary: Building The Muscle For Tech Sovereignty: Critical Minerals Must Underpin India’s Semiconductor and Manufacturing Ambition  Swarajya
articles.full_text:
The momentum at Semicon India 2026 signals a fundamental maturity and inflection point. Capital commitments under ISM 2.0 (Indian Semiconductor Mission), Applied Materials’ $5-billion India Vision 2035, Lam Research’s silicon-component expansions, and Tata Electronics’ materials and advanced packaging partnerships confirm that India is moving beyond peripheral assembly into the core semiconductor value chain.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s emphasis on India as a trusted manufacturing partner, coupled with an explicit focus on equipment, specialty chemicals and advanced packaging, correctly acknowledges that fabs do not operate in isolation.
Yet the viability of India’s sunrise ambitions hinges on a less visible foundation: critical minerals and rare-earth midstream processing.
Domestic semiconductor demand is projected to approach $200 billion by 2035, yet 90–95 per cent of current requirements remain import-dependent. The same vulnerability shadows India’s electric mobility push. An EV traction motor depends on sintered neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) permanent magnets, which also power wind turbines, robotics, aerospace actuators and precision radar systems. Nearly 95 per cent of the economic value in the rare-earth chain sits at the magnet and component stage.
India is not short of geology. It holds the world’s third-largest rare-earth reserves. The real constraint is midstream processing; cracking, chemical separation, metallisation, and alloying. In 2025, permanent-magnet imports crossed $300 million, with China supplying roughly 70–80 per cent. When Beijing tightened export controls on heavy rare earths in early 2025, Indian EV platforms and precision component makers faced immediate delays, forced substitutions and margin pressure. Concentrated midstream supply chains can stall an entire industrial corridor overnight.
Historically, domestic output has been limited by structural friction. State miner IREL operates beach-sand and monazite operations at OSCOM in Odisha and Chavara in Kerala, but monazite is classified as a prescribed substance under the Atomic Energy Act because of its thorium content. This regulatory perimeter constrained private capital in upstream extraction for years. Legacy facilities were also designed for basic separation rather than high-purity heavy rare-earth refining or sintered magnet alloys. As IREL leadership has noted, India has ample ore; what it has lacked is an integrated midstream and downstream ecosystem.
National policy is now moving to close the gap. The National Critical Mineral Mission, the ₹7,280-crore Rare Earth Permanent Magnet scheme targeting 6,000 tonnes of sintered NdFeB capacity, and four dedicated Rare Earth Corridors across Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala provide the industrial framework. Physical connectivity is improving too: dedicated freight corridors linking coastal placer deposits in Odisha to inland processing parks, ports and manufacturing hubs are beginning to remove long-standing logistical penalties.
Private enterprise is responding in parallel. Hyderabad-based Nexon Geochem is building integrated facilities to move from oxide to sintered NdFeB magnets for EVs, clean energy and defence. Lohum has begun extracting lithium in Zimbabwe, the first Indian company to secure overseas hard-rock assets, and plans to refine the material in India while developing magnet and battery-recycling capacity. Alongside state acquisitions through KABIL and circular-economy players such as BatX Energies, industry is pursuing a two-track approach: securing overseas feedstock while anchoring midstream processing at home.
Technology sovereignty cannot rest on unilateral self-reliance alone. It requires disciplined, multi-aligned partnerships. Frameworks with the United States, Australia and Japan through the Minerals Security Partnership and the Quad provide important, diversified pathways.
In this context, India’s tie-up with Russia is also a complementary and strategic pillar, which needs to be leveraged extensively. Beyond large unexploited deposits such as Tomtor, it retains deep separation and metallurgy expertise through institutes like Rosatom’s Giredmet. Recent engagements, including Giredmet’s technology partnerships with Nexon Geochem and collaboration with TEXMIN at IIT (ISM) Dhanbad, show that the runway for processing technology transfer and domestic NdFeB manufacturing is open. Access to Russian high-purity separation know-how can accelerate Indian capability, provided projects are structured with clear compliance, bankable offtakes and commercial discipline.
True industrial sovereignty is not won on final assembly lines. It is secured through control over the processing platforms, metallurgical standards and material inputs that feed those lines.
To convert the promise of Semicon India into durable capability, India needs to:
--Fast-track critical-mineral processing clusters and integrate them with Dedicated Freight Corridors, SEZs, industrial clusters and deep-water ports.
--Convert bilateral MoUs into bankable joint ventures with technology licensing, risk-sharing and firm domestic offtake.
--Align ISM 2.0 incentives with the NCMM so that chemical inputs, magnet plants and silicon fabs scale together. NCMM is National Critical Minerals Mission.
--Institutionalise closed-loop recycling to turn scrap electronics and spent batteries into secondary strategic reserves.
India has the market scale, political stability and engineering depth to anchor global technology supply chains. Building the domestic midstream muscle to process its own critical inputs is the decisive test of this decade. This is the non-negotiable foundation for genuine tech sovereignty.
Sanjay Srivastava is a Strategic Advisor and Global Ecosystem Builder with nearly three decades of leadership experience across Mahindra World City, Tata Group, and Accenture. He advises corporations, government bodies and investors on manufacturing platforms, critical minerals and cross-border industrial alliances.

articles.title: The Starship spacecraft completed its first orbital flight, deploying Starlink satellites into orbit - Українські Національні Новини (УНН)
articles.summary: The Starship spacecraft completed its first orbital flight, deploying Starlink satellites into orbit  Українські Національні Новини (УНН)
articles.full_text:
Kyiv • UNN
Starship reached orbit for the first time and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites despite an engine failure. The mission was shortened from 10 hours to 3.
On Monday, SpaceX's giant Starship rocket reached orbit for the first time and deployed new Starlink satellites into orbit, achieving important milestones despite an engine malfunction early in the flight and the decision to shorten the mission by seven hours, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The mission was supposed to last 10 hours, but after engine problems arose, it was shortened to three hours. This flight from the Texas launch site was the rocket's fourteenth since 2023; Elon Musk's company plans to begin regular operations with it this year.
Unlike previous Starship flights, Monday's mission was not merely a test of a next-generation rocket but also an operational task involving the deployment into orbit of Starlink satellites worth millions of dollars. This made it the first revenue-generating Starship mission, although the spacecraft's final design is still under development.
SpaceX shares, which had previously risen by nearly 9% from their IPO price, fell by about 1% on Monday. A significant portion of SpaceX's market value and investors' confidence in the company—which was valued at $2 trillion as of Friday's market close—depends on the success of Starship, the world's first fully reusable spacecraft.
The unmanned vehicle, as tall as a 40-story building and consisting of the Super Heavy booster and the main upper stage mounted on it (the Starship spacecraft itself), lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase complex on the Gulf Coast near the city of Brownsville.
The Super Heavy booster carried Starship's upper stage into space, after which it returned to the waters of the Gulf of Mexico, making a controlled splashdown (the booster's previous two landing attempts ended in hard impacts with the surface). According to SpaceX, some of the booster's engines shut down during its descent.
After reaching space, one of Starship's three main engines shut down prematurely; as a result, SpaceX representative Dan Huot announced during the mission's livestream that the spacecraft would not be able to reach orbit.
"The team has decided not to go to orbit," Huot said. However, a few minutes later, Huot changed the decision after engineers reported that the vehicle could still try to ignite the other onboard engines to reach orbit—which Starship successfully did shortly afterward.
We would add
Once in orbit, Starship deployed 26 next-generation Starlink satellites one after another at an altitude of approximately 269 km (161 miles), marking the first time the spacecraft had deployed a payload in orbit.
"All 26 operational Starlink V3 satellites have been deployed, and they are functioning nominally," Musk wrote on the social media platform X.
"Deploying all 26 Starlink V3 satellites into their target orbit is a huge achievement, especially given that this is the first commercial Starship flight to generate revenue," said Dean Slayden, a quality control manager and aerospace engineer at Accu Components. "But from an engineering perspective, the most interesting moment was how the team handled the engine failure during ascent."
The publication notes that engine problems also occurred during some of Starship's previous suborbital flights; this is a longstanding issue for the program involving a critically important aspect—the rocket's ability to maneuver in space. Although this capability is less important for deploying Starlink satellites into low Earth orbit, it is crucial for Starship's future missions, including delivering NASA astronauts to the Moon.
Jared Isaacman congratulated SpaceX on the social media platform X for managing "to get the ship to orbit and complete every phase of the flight safely, responsibly, and, most importantly, inspiringly."
The controlled descent of Starship into the waters of the Pacific Ocean—seven hours earlier than scheduled—ended with an engine maneuver that turned the vehicle into a vertical position for a nose-up splashdown. At the moment it touched the ocean’s surface, flames engulfed the rocket’s base; it subsequently tipped onto its side, followed by a powerful explosion that produced a large fireball. The company had not planned to recover and reuse the spacecraft after the mission.
Context
Starship was created to enable more frequent launches of SpaceX’s Starlink satellites and to carry out future NASA missions to the Moon. Reaching orbit—a key measure of the success of any new rocket intended to deliver payloads into space—was a long-awaited achievement for Starship. Musk once predicted that this would happen as early as 2022, with satellite launches following in 2023.
All 13 previous Starship test flights, conducted since 2023, had been limited to suborbital space as part of a development campaign that has lasted nearly a decade and cost SpaceX more than $15 billion. Musk said that in the future he plans to conduct hundreds or even thousands of Starship flights per year—launch rates unprecedented in the space industry.
"We are 2–3 years away from Starship flights at one-hour intervals," Musk wrote on the social network X on Sunday.

articles.title: ASML Sold Nothing in Europe in 2026: Chip-Tool Demand Gap Exposes EU Supply-Only Strategy - Tech Times
articles.summary: ASML Sold Nothing in Europe in 2026: Chip-Tool Demand Gap Exposes EU Supply-Only Strategy  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Europe spent tens of billions of euros on a semiconductor sovereignty plan, and the world's only maker of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) chip-printing machines earned nothing on the continent in return. ASML, the Dutch lithography giant that controls every advanced chipmaking node above 5 nanometers (nm), reported zero European revenue in each of the first two quarters of 2026 — down from 5% in 2024, 4% in 2023, and 1% in 2025. Speaking at De Balie, Amsterdam's prominent political and cultural center, on September 21, ASML Executive Vice President for Global Public Affairs Frank Heemskerk named the cause directly: Europe is not building the kind of chip factories that would buy his company's most advanced tools. "We are selling absolutely nothing in Europe," he said. "Because Europe is not investing and because no chip factories are being built in Europe. That is genuinely worrying." Bloomberg reported September 22 on Heemskerk's panel discussion in Amsterdam the previous evening.
From Five Percent to Zero in Three Years
The decline is not a rounding error. Europe accounted for 5% of ASML's net system sales in 2024, 4% in 2023, 2% in 2022, and 1% in 2025. By the first two quarters of 2026, that figure hit zero. ASML's quarterly regional breakdown for Q2 2026 showed South Korea leading at 43%, Taiwan at 30%, China at 14%, the United States at 9%, and Japan at 4%. Europe registered nothing.
The backdrop makes the contrast starker. Globally, ASML is having a record year. The company raised its full-year 2026 net sales guidance twice — from an initial range of €34 billion to €39 billion (approximately $38.7 billion to $44.4 billion) to €36 billion to €40 billion (approximately $41 billion to $45.5 billion) after Q1 results, and then all the way to €43 billion to €45 billion (approximately $48.9 billion to $51.2 billion) after Q2. AI-driven chip demand is outpacing manufacturing capacity, and the world's foundries are competing aggressively for ASML's production slots. CEO Christophe Fouquet said after the Q2 2026 earnings report that ASML is "pretty much already close" to receiving all EUV orders it needs for 2027 while exploring a further 30% capacity expansion for 2028.
ASML, Europe's largest company by market capitalization at approximately $660 billion, is thriving everywhere except its home continent.
What EUV Lithography Is and Why Europe Cannot Order Any
To understand the zero, it helps to understand the machine.
EUV lithography uses 13.5 nm wavelength light — generated by firing a high-powered CO₂ laser at a stream of tiny tin droplets to create a plasma — and reflects that light off multilayer mirrors made of alternating molybdenum and silicon layers, in a vacuum, to print transistor patterns on silicon wafers. Each machine weighs approximately 200 metric tons (441,000 lbs), consumes roughly 10 times more electrical power than a conventional deep-ultraviolet (DUV) immersion tool, and in its standard production form costs approximately $180 million to $360 million per unit. ASML is the only company on the planet that makes them commercially. Its High-NA EUV system, the Twinscan EXE:5000, operates at a numerical aperture of 0.55 and is used for chips at 2 nm and below; the next generation — hyper-NA EUV — could reach approximately $720 million per unit by around 2030.
EUV is required for the smallest, most capable transistor nodes: 5 nm, 3 nm, 2 nm, and below. These are the nodes used in leading-edge AI processors, advanced mobile chips, and high-bandwidth memory. Every fab that wants to manufacture at those nodes must have ASML machines. There is no alternative.
The critical point is that none of the active European semiconductor manufacturing projects are targeting those nodes. Every European fab currently under construction or recently opened uses older, less expensive deep-ultraviolet (DUV) tools — capable machines for automotive-grade and industrial chips, but ones that ASML's leading-edge EUV division simply does not supply. The technical reason is straightforward: fabs targeting 12 nm, 16 nm, 22 nm, or 28 nm nodes have no need for 13.5 nm photons. DUV at 193 nm, used in immersion lithography, is sufficient for those feature sizes and far cheaper to operate.
That is the EUV demand gap in its most basic form: Europe is investing in semiconductor production, but in the tier of semiconductor production that does not require ASML's most advanced products.
What Is Actually Being Built in Europe
The existing European investment is substantial in dollar terms and real in strategic value for the specific markets it targets. It simply does not produce the demand ASML is waiting for.
Intel's Fab 34, located near Leixlip, Ireland, operates on Intel 3 and Intel 4 process technologies. Intel recently committed €5 billion (approximately $5.7 billion) to expand the Leixlip campus and increase production of Xeon processors — a direct follow-on from the company's decision to abandon its much larger planned investment in Magdeburg, Germany, and Wroclaw, Poland.
The European Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (ESMC), the joint venture between TSMC, Bosch, Infineon, and NXP backed by €5 billion in German state aid, is building a €15 billion (approximately $17.1 billion) fab near Dresden. At full capacity in 2029, it will process around 480,000 wafers per year on automotive and industrial processes including 28 nm and 12/16 nm nodes — producing automotive and industrial semiconductors that European manufacturers need and cannot currently source domestically.
Infineon opened its new €5 billion (approximately $5.7 billion) Smart Power Fab in Dresden in July 2026, marking the largest single investment in the company's history and doubling its on-site output capacity for power semiconductors and analog chips.
GlobalFoundries broke ground in March 2026 on an expansion of its existing Fab 1 in Dresden targeting specialty processes including 22 nm FD-SOI (22FDX) and embedded non-volatile memory.
These investments are genuinely significant for the automotive and industrial chip segments they serve. None, however, involves EUV lithography. None is building the type of leading-edge foundry that TSMC, Samsung, or Intel's most advanced operations require. And none signals that a European hyperscaler, European AI hardware company, or European defense establishment is prepared to commit to purchasing chips produced in a European EUV-equipped fab.
That last point is the one Heemskerk has been pressing in Brussels.
Why Demand Must Come Before the Fab
Heemskerk's argument at De Balie went beyond cataloging the absence of European fab activity. He argued that the EU's Chips Act strategy has the causation reversed — it is trying to create chip supply and hoping demand will follow, when the economics of advanced semiconductor manufacturing require the opposite.
"There simply is no demand here for these kinds of highly specialized machines," he said. "That is the problem. So apart from trying to attract investment with capital on the supply side, we should do much more to create demand." ASML has been pressing the case directly with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, urging EU authorities to use their collective market power to aggregate demand for locally manufactured chips across European industries.
The logic is identical to the mechanism used in European defense procurement: governments commit collectively to buying from domestic producers, which gives those producers a bankable revenue forecast, which makes the capital investment in production capacity economically rational. Without that committed customer base, no private company will build a leading-edge fab on speculation, and no bank will finance one.
Industry analysts have noted this structural problem in assessments of the EU Chips Act: a supply-side strategy that cannot secure customer commitments from European AI developers, data center operators, and defense procurement agencies leaves European fabs without the long-term order books that justify the multi-billion-euro capital expenditure.
Heemskerk said ASML is also fielding aggressive courtship from the US, China, and India — each offering to host expansions of ASML's manufacturing and research operations. Washington, where ASML already conducts approximately a quarter of its research, has asked whether that share could rise to half. China and India, he said, are "rolling out the reddest of red carpets." Heemskerk described this competitive pressure in his Amsterdam appearance, urging Europe to respond before ASML's expansion goes elsewhere.
Why Europe's Existing Fabs Still Don't Solve the Problem
Even setting aside the EUV node gap, a compounding structural barrier undermines the strategic case for European chip sovereignty: the packaging problem. Modern semiconductor manufacturing does not end at the wafer fabrication step. Once a wafer is produced, it must be cut into individual dies, packaged, tested, and integrated into finished modules — a set of processes handled by outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) facilities. Europe has largely lost its domestic OSAT capacity, which means that chips produced at European fabs — including Intel's Leixlip wafers and ESMC's planned output — routinely travel to Asian facilities in Taiwan, South Korea, or Malaysia for final assembly and testing before being shipped back to European customers.
This means that even a genuine ramp in European wafer production would not produce the strategic outcome the EU Chips Act was designed to achieve: a complete semiconductor value chain on European soil that cannot be disrupted by geopolitical events in the Taiwan Strait or the South China Sea. A "Made in Europe" chip remains a claim that requires heavy asterisking as long as the chip's final assembly happens in Asia.
The European Court of Auditors (ECA) issued a sobering verdict on the first Chips Act's progress in 2025: the EU is highly unlikely to reach its 20% global mark

articles.title: The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector
articles.summary: The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved form of lie detector, according to a Department of Defense budget request. The program, called Polygraph+ or Polygraph Next, will focus on scoring algorithms that use artificial intelligence and machine learning and on a technique called “standoff sensing,” which…
articles.full_text:
The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved form of lie detector, according to a Department of Defense budget request. The program, called Polygraph+ or Polygraph Next, will focus on scoring algorithms that use artificial intelligence and machine learning and on a technique called “standoff sensing,” which refers to the ability to take physiological readings without attaching a device to a subject’s person.



According to details of the budget document, which were first reported by Inside Defense, the project will “modernize federal polygraph and credibility assessment technologies” to improve their accuracy and reliability. But the project may be just the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies. “It’s a misguided effort to reduce the complex to something that is tangible,” says Kyri Kotsoglou, a legal scholar at Northumbria University in the UK who studies the use of polygraphs in the justice system.



The move comes at a time of high tension within the department. Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has been increasingly turning to polygraph tests in an attempt to find the sources of alleged leaks to the press. In September, the New York Times reported that around 50 officers on the Joint Staff had been given polygraph tests after news coverage reported on the depletion of US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran. 



Polygraph+ will be run by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which conducts background checks for the federal government. According to the budget document, which has not yet been approved by Congress, the new technology will be used for vetting of prospective employees and “insider threat detection.” It is not yet clear which specific technologies will be used, and the DCSA did not respond to a request for more information. 



But other Pentagon efforts offer potential clues. In 2023, the department’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) ran an open submission process to find companies with products that could be used for deception detection.



It selected two companies to build prototypes: Presage Technologies, which claims to be able to measure heart rate and breathing rate using standard cameras, and Altec Research, a medical sensor company now branching out into non-contact sensing technologies. A screenshot of Altec’s prototype technology released by the DIU shows that it tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity. Presage Technologies and Altec Research did not respond to requests for comment. The DIU declined to comment. 



Altec Research has built a prototype that tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity. ALTEC RESEARCH




Current lie detection technology has barely changed since the polygraph was invented in the 1920s. Examiners rely on blood pressure, pulse, breathing, and sweat measurements to determine if someone is lying. They make judgments about the veracity of respondents’ replies on the basis of differences in their physiological response to baseline questions like “Is the sky blue?” and target questions like “Have you ever committed a crime?”



The federal government conducts tens of thousands of the tests each year while screening employees, but the reliability of this technology has been repeatedly challenged—and its results are rarely admissible in court. In 1983, Congress’s Office of Technology Assessment concluded that there was very limited evidence supporting the polygraph’s use for screening employees, and in 2003, the US National Research Council (NRC) said evidence for its efficacy was “weak at best.” 



Research suggests humans can spot a lie just over half the time without any technical assistance. The American Polygraph Association claims the polygraph is between 80% and 94% accurate. But the 2003 NRC report pointed out that a screening test with this level of accuracy could still lead to a lot of mistakes. The DOD employs 2.8 million people; an imperfect system applied at that scale could end up falsely accusing tens of thousands.



There are other issues too. Polygraph interpretations are often subjective: Different examiners get wildly different results, and people from minority groups are more likely to be judged as deceptive. What’s more, with training it’s possible for interviewees to learn a variety of countermeasures that can help beat the test; for example, they may artificially heighten their physiological response to baseline questions by stepping on a pin hidden in their shoe. 



“If you know how it works, you can beat it,” says Sophie van der Zee, an associate professor who studies deception at Erasmus University in Rotterdam. She says the machine’s biggest effect is deterrence—often, subjects confess before it even begins. “But that only works if people think a polygraph works,” she points out.





Various new strategies for lie detection have been attempted over the decades, with technologies ranging from thermal cameras to pupil trackers to brain scans. None of them have yielded reliable results outside the lab. The problem is that there’s no single telltale sign of lying that’s true for everyone all the time. “There is still no Pinocchio’s nose,” says van der Zee. 



AI could theoretically improve polygraphs if it could find patterns in the data that examiners can’t. AI algorithms are also more likely to be used for “multi-modal” deception detection, which seeks to combine multiple measurements into an overall deception “score” that is harder for people to game. Three things are happening under the surface that lie detection tries to home in on, van der Zee says: physiological stress, cognitive load, and the conscious efforts people make to conceal the fact that they’re lying. Current polygraph technology tackles only one.“The more you can have combined methods that approach it from these three different angles, the more successful you will be,” van der Zee says. This isn’t a new concept—in the 2000s, researchers at Manchester Metropolitan University in the UK developed a system called Silent Talker that generated a deception score from video footage. This was later folded into iBorderCtrl, an EU-funded pilot program. In the US, a project called AVATAR incorporated eye tracking, voice analysis, and body movement detection into a tool for use at border crossings. All these projects have quietly faded away. 



Kotsoglou says combining AI and the polygraph is “the worst of both worlds” because it adds uncertainty on top of invalidity. Even if AI or machine learning can spot previously unseen patterns in physiological data, it won’t be able to reliably link them to lying because there is no real ground truth. 



“Even if you have all the records in the world from polygraph tests, you don’t know whether those polygraph tests are right or not,” says Marion Oswald, a professor of law who has written with Kotsoglou on the use of polygraphs in the justice system. She fears that new forms of lie detection will, like the polygraph, be used more as a psychological prop than a scientific tool. 



“It seems very much a response to the concern of the current administration to leaks and perceived lack of loyalty,” says Oswald. “[Lie detection is] being used as a threat, to intimidate and force people to confess to things, as opposed to anything that’s actually getting valid information.”

articles.summary: Review: Silent Hill: Townfall Largely Delivers on PS5 and Pro, Falls Short on PC  Digital FoundrySilent Hill: Townfall Performance Benchmark Review - 35 GPUs Tested  TechPowerUpSilent Hill Townfall: Iconic horror game gets a clever Scottish makeover  BBC“Silent Hill: Townfall” Gets Fogged in by Frustrating Gameplay  Roger EbertHow to Get the Dog Ending  IGN
articles.full_text:
The latest release in the iconic horror series, Silent Hill: Townfall, has finally arrived on PlayStation consoles and PC. While we were unable to produce a day-one review due to an exceptionally busy release schedule and staff shortages, the game is well worth briefly covering in written form - and indeed, in this week's DF Direct (embedded above).
Visually, Townfall is a strikingly handsome game that masterfully captures the eerie, suffocating atmosphere expected of the series, in a rarer first-person perspective. It shares notable artistic commonalities with recent entries like the Silent Hill 2 remake, particularly through its use of high-quality volumetric fog, rich indirect diffuse lighting and highly detailed environment modelling that elevates the overall sense of dread - this time, in Scotland.
The game sets itself apart technically by using hardware-accelerated Lumen across all configurations, even performance mode. This results in significantly more convincing reflections than those seen in titles relying solely on software-based solutions, replacing blobby, indistinct forms with clearly defined, polygonal representations of the game world.
Despite the impressive lighting tech, there are minor curiosities in the presentation. The player character remains absent from reflections, likely a pragmatic choice to avoid the complexities of third-person animation in a first-person title, or alternatively to sidestep the visual limitations that often arise when rendering character models at high levels of detail in reflective surfaces.
Performance on PS5 is generally solid, though there are some minor, irritating instances of traversal stutter, which remains a common complaint with Unreal Engine 5 titles. These drops are mostly confined to cinematic cutscenes and are often subtle enough that they can be mitigated by using system-level VRR support, though they remain an unwelcome distraction.
Resolution metrics reveal a clear hierarchy across the Sony hardware. The base PS5 in quality mode has an internal resolution between 1080p and 1152p, while the performance mode dips to roughly 792p to 864p, leading to noticeable shimmering in high-contrast scenes. Conversely, the PlayStation 5 Pro offers a significant boost, with quality mode at ~1620p and performance mode at ~1215p. With PSSR enabled, we get a fixed 1440p base resolution in quality mode and 864p in performance mode, slightly lower internal resolutions that nonetheless resolve into greater detail, less noise and better temporal stability, thanks to the advantages of PSSR over the default TSR used elsewhere.
On the PC front, the experience is initially impressive before awful technical problems manifest. While a mid-range card like the RTX 4060 can achieve a respectable frame rate at 1440p settings - and even runs reasonably well at 4K in DLSS performance mode with RT off - the title is marred by egregious shader compilation stutter, alongside a worse rendition of the traversal stutter we spotted on console. This technical friction is particularly detrimental to a horror game, where the constant flow of atmospheric dread is easily shattered by sudden, jarring frame-time spikes. This isn't the sort of scare that I signed up for.
Furthermore, the PC version lacks integrated frame generation, which is a bizarre omission for an Unreal Engine 5 title given that support is baked into the engine. It also looks like older DLSS CNN-based Model F is being forced, despite the game shipping with the Transformer-based DLSS 4.0 DLL file. FSR 3 frame generation can be enabled via third-party mods. It's also necessary to edit configuration files to disable film grain or chromatic aberration, with no menu options for these marmite effects. There are also ReShade add-ons to disable cutscene letterboxing and mods to adjust FOV settings, if desired; PC Gaming Wiki and NexusMods are good resources to see additional PC options.
Ultimately, Silent Hill: Townfall is an aesthetically masterful game that captures the essence of the series with great care, priced fairly for its scale (£45/$50 puts it well below usual triple-A fare). However, the recurring technical issues - especially the performance issues and limitations on PC - need urgent attention. Until these patches arrive, the game doesn't quite deserve a full-throated endorsement.

articles.summary: Korea’s semiconductor boom sends 2026 tax revenue to record high  Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.full_text:
Government estimates tax revenue will reach 478.6 trillion won ($353.7 billion) as chip profits and a bullish stock market fuel an unprecedented windfall.
Published
The Ministry of Finance and EconomyYONHAP
Korea's tax revenue is estimated to reach a record 478.6 trillion won ($353.7 billion) this year, driven by the semiconductor supercycle, government data showed Wednesday.
The figure marks an increase of 104.7 trillion won from the previous year's 373.9 trillion won, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy. The previous record was 395.9 trillion won in 2022.
The revised estimate is 88.4 trillion won higher than the original projection used to draw up the 2026 budget.
"Tax revenue has far exceeded the initial estimate due to the semiconductor boom and the bullish stock market, both of which were difficult to predict," a finance ministry official said.
"Operating profits in the chip industry were around 70 to 80 percent higher than originally projected," the official added.
The finance ministry said corporate tax revenue is expected to reach 136.4 trillion won this year, up 51.8 trillion won from 2025.
The combined operating profit of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix for this year is currently projected by the market at around 638 trillion won, compared with 339 trillion won forecast in February.
The government projected income tax revenue would reach 152.4 trillion won, up from the initial forecast of 132 trillion won, driven by higher bonus payments at semiconductor and financial companies.
Securities transaction tax revenue is expected to reach 12.4 trillion won, up from the original estimate of 5.4 trillion won, buoyed by a bullish stock market in the first half of this year.
Based on the revised estimates, experts said more than 200 trillion won could be available for the Future Fund, which the government plans to launch next year to channel an unprecedented tax revenue windfall from the semiconductor boom into sustainable economic growth.
The calculation is based on projected surplus tax revenue of 56.2 trillion won, in addition to the windfall revenue of 162.3 trillion won.
"The bill on the Future Fund submitted to the National Assembly stipulates that surplus revenue can be transferred to the fund," the official said, noting that relevant ministries are discussing how to use the surplus.
Korea earlier introduced the concept of "windfall revenue," referring to tax revenue exceeding its long-term trend due to structural economic changes or significant economic fluctuations, such as an industrial supercycle.
The government said the concept differs from surplus tax revenue, which refers to tax receipts exceeding official forecasts due to unexpected short-term economic fluctuations or forecasting errors.
